claims.assertion: The driver never reached my pickup point: his closest approach was 545 m (F1) and he never entered the 200 m pickup range, so the platform's own arrival record is null (F4).

The driver's "I'm Here" tap does not satisfy NS-1: he pressed it at 12:05:55 while 601 m from the pickup point and spent 0 seconds inside 200 m after the tap (F5), contradicting his statement that he waited at the pickup (F12).

The driver's claimed 3-minute wait was served 600 m away from the pickup point, stationary 12:05:35–12:09:05 (F2), so the NS-1 requirement of waiting at the pickup point for over 3 minutes is not met.
Because NS-1 (i)(ii)(iii) all fail, the $6.61 cancellation fee was wrongly charged and must be refunded in full; the fee is on record in the fare data as $6.61 (F7, F3) with no surge involved (F8).

The driver tapped "I'm Here" while GPS shows he was not at the pickup point (F5 vs F1), which is the abuse-of-cancellation/waiting-button pattern that warrants an additional account flag for the driver under NS-2.

My chat message at 12:06 saying I was at the pickup point and saw no car (F10) is consistent with the GPS record that the driver was hundreds of metres away, and the driver's "waited more than 3 min" message (F11) came while he was stationary 600 m from the pickup point (F2).
My client's clean record — 3.7-year account, 4.7 rating, zero no-show disputes upheld in 90 days (F16) — supports that this dispute is genuine rather than a rider-attempted fee dodge.

No traffic or weather condition could explain the driver stopping 600 m short of the pickup point: no speed-band records and no incidents were registered on the route during the trip window, and weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain (F13, F14, F15).

weaknesses: The timeline contains two mutually inconsistent entries: F5 says the driver tapped "I'm Here" at 12:05:55, while F6 says he never tapped it at all — the judge may treat the "arrival" act as unproven, which still defeats the driver's case but changes the factual narrative.

The driver does have a long, well-rated record (F17: 2.4-year account, 4.84 rating, 502 trips, 0 upheld disputes), so the judge may see this as a one-off GPS/anomaly rather than the deliberate fee abuse our flag request (C5) implies.

My own location during the wait is not directly evidenced in the GPS facts; my presence at the pickup point rests on the chat message F10 alone, and chat is user-submitted content that loses to system records where they conflict.

claims.assertion: The GPS record is the decisive evidence on the arrival requirement: the driver's closest approach to the pickup point was 545 m and he never entered the 200 m arrival radius, so the 'I'm Here' condition of NS-1(ii) is not met.

The driver tapped 'I'm Here' at 12:05:55 while 601 m from the pickup point and then remained inside the pickup radius for 0 seconds, so even if the tap occurred, the required on-location waiting time under NS-1(iii) was never accumulated.

The timeline contains contradictory arrival entries — driver_arrived_at is null, and the record also shows driver_pressed_here_at as null — i.e. the platform never recorded an arrival; this reinforces that NS-1(i) and (ii) are not satisfied.
The driver's stationary period of 3 min 30 s ran from 12:05:35 to 12:09:05 at a location 600 m from the pickup point, not at the pickup point, so NS-1(ii) fails regardless of the length of the stop.

Even on the driver's own account — chat message at 12:06 'I'm here already, silver Toyota Altis, please come out' and the 12:08 message 'Waited more than 3 min, cancelling' — the claimed waiting occurred where the GPS places the vehicle, 600 m away; the rider's reply that she was at the pickup point and saw no car is consistent with the GPS record.

Because NS-1(i)(ii)(iii) are not all satisfied, the $6.61 no-show cancellation fee does not stand and must be refunded in full to the rider (voucher form, within the 30-day window still open as the trip was cancelled 12:09:05 and the dispute is filed now).
The $6.61 was charged without surge and with no additional fare items attached, so the entire disputed amount is the single cancellation fee and there is nothing to net off in the refund calculation.

Road conditions offer no justification for the vehicle stopping 600 m short: no speed-band records and no traffic incidents were recorded on the route during the trip window, and the weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain.

The rider's account (3.7 years, rating 4.7, zero disputes and zero upheld in 90 days) is consistent with a rider who genuinely attended the pickup point; this is context only and does not by itself decide the case.

A flag_account under NS-2 is a discretionary consequence of a false 'I'm Here' declaration; the driver nevertheless has a clean 90-day record (502 trips, 0 disputes, 0 upheld), and the array of system records here — null arrival, null here-tap, never within 200 m — indicates a GPS/app-side recording problem rather than proof of deliberate abuse, so we ask the judge to make the refund the finding and to treat any account referral as non-adverse.

weaknesses: The driver's own written statement (F12) and chat messages F9 and F11 assert he pressed 'I'm Here' and waited more than 3 minutes at the pickup; the other side will lead with these to argue he did what NS-1 requires, and the timeline entry F5 records such a tap at 12:05:55.

The driver did actually tap at 12:05:55 (F5) and sat stationary for 3 min 30 s (F2), so the other side can argue the waiting element of NS-1(iii) was met in substance; our rebuttal depends entirely on the 601 m / 600 m distance measurements in F1, F2 and F5.

The timeline is internally inconsistent — F5 records a here-tap while F6 says driver_pressed_here_at is null — so the judge may treat the arrival-button record as unreliable; that cuts both ways because if the tap record is unreliable, the driver's assertion that he was at the pickup could also be argued as merely unreliably recorded.
